newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean banks' bad loans rise 6.5 percent in '96.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean banks' bad loans rise 6.5 percent in '96.

text.p: Outstanding bad loans held by South Korea's 25 commercial banks rose 6.5 percent to 2.44 trillion won at the end of 1996 from 2.29 trillion a year earlier, the Bank of Korea said on Wednesday.
But the ratio of bad loans to total loans of the 25 banks -- 15 nationwide banks and 10 regional banks -- dropped slightly to 0.8 percent from 0.9 percent, the bank's statement said.

"Despite the rise in bad loans, we can't say the situation worsened because bank loans as a whole increased faster," said Lee Suk-keun, deputy director at the central bank's supervisory planning division.
The bank said commercial banks' outstanding loan loss reserves stood at 3.42 trillion won at the end of 1996, up 8.0 percent from 3.16 trillion a year before.
The ratio of their net worth to risk-weighted assets on a Bank for International Settlements (BIS) basis fell to 9.14 percent at the end of 1996 from 9.33 percent a year before, the bank said.
"Banks had trouble in increasing capital last year because of a slump in the stock market," Lee said.
The central bank earlier said combined operating profits of the commercial banks rose 16.2 pct to 4.17 trillion won in calendar 1996 from 3.59 trillion in 1995.
Interest income rose 25.2 percent to 7.31 trillion won, contributing to the rise in operating profits, the bank said.
But net profits fell 2.4 percent to 846.8 billion won in 1996 from 867.6 billion in 1995 due to losses from investment in securities, it said.
The central bank said the book value of the banks' securities holdings fell by an estimated 895.2 billion won. The value fell by 543.7 billion in 1995.
Lee said a slump in the Seoul bourse was to blame for the rise. The composite stock index closed 1996 at a year low of 651.22, sharply lower from 882.94 at the start of the year.
